lead: This unit adds geometry to vectors: length, angle, perpendicularity. After it you can build an orthonormal basis, project a vector onto a subspace, fit a least-squares line, and read a matrix through its QR and SVD factorizations.
about: Chapter 5.1 defines the inner product and the norm it produces. Chapter 5.2 uses the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to bound angles and to prove the triangle inequality. Chapter 5.3 defines orthogonal and orthonormal sets and the orthogonal complement of a subspace. Chapter 5.4 builds an orthonormal basis from any basis by the Gram–Schmidt process. Chapter 5.5 uses that basis to project a vector onto a subspace and to solve least-squares problems. Chapter 5.6 reads Gram–Schmidt as the matrix factorization A = QR. Chapter 5.7 generalizes to A = UΣVᵀ, the SVD, which exists for every matrix. Each chapter uses the one before it, and the numbers in 5.1 recur in 5.2, 5.4 and 5.6 so you can check the arithmetic across chapters.

chapters.idea: An inner product is a rule that assigns a number to each pair of vectors and from it we get length, distance and angle.
chapters.depth: Define the inner product axiomatically over ℝ and over ℂ: positive definiteness ⟨u,u⟩ ≥ 0 with equality only for u = 0, conjugate symmetry, and linearity in the first slot. Give three examples: the standard dot product on ℝⁿ, a weighted inner product ⟨u,v⟩ = Σ wᵢuᵢvᵢ with cᵢ > 0, and the integral inner product ⟨f,g⟩ = ∫₀¹ f(x)g(x)dx on polynomials. Build the norm ‖u‖ = √⟨u,u⟩ and list its properties: ‖cu‖ = |c|‖u‖, distance d(u,v) = ‖u − v‖, unit vectors, and cos θ = ⟨u,v⟩/(‖u‖‖v‖). Work in ℝ², ℝ³ and simple polynomial spaces only. Some syllabi call the inner product the scalar product or dot product.

figure.title: From inner product to angle
figure.aria: A four-box flow showing that a pair of vectors gives an inner product, the inner product gives a norm, and both give the cosine of the angle.

chapters.trap: Over ℂ the inner product is conjugate-linear in the second slot, so ⟨u,v⟩ is the conjugate of ⟨v,u⟩, not equal to it; and ‖u‖ is the square root of ⟨u,u⟩, never ⟨u,u⟩ itself.
chapters.leave: The inequalities to 5.2; orthogonality and its uses to 5.3 onwards.

chapters.idea: No inner product can exceed the product of the two lengths, and that single bound produces the triangle inequality for norms.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. State the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality |⟨u,v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖, prove it from ‖u − tv‖² ≥ 0 with t = ⟨u,v⟩/‖v‖², and state the equality case: equality holds exactly when one vector is a scalar multiple of the other, or one of them is 0. Derive the triangle inequality ‖u + v‖ ≤ ‖u‖ + ‖v‖ from it. State the Pythagorean relation ‖u + v‖² = ‖u‖² + ‖v‖² for orthogonal u and v, and the parallelogram law ‖u + v‖² + ‖u − v‖² = 2‖u‖² + 2‖v‖². Some syllabi call the first result the Cauchy–Bunyakovsky–Schwarz inequality. One numerical check, no long proofs.

figure.title: One inequality, four results
figure.aria: A flow chart with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality at the top leading to the angle bound and the triangle inequality, and a second branch where orthogonality gives Pythagoras and then the parallelogram law.

chapters.example: With u = (1, 2, 2) and v = (3, 0, 4): ⟨u,v⟩ = 11 and ‖u‖‖v‖ = 3 × 5 = 15, so 11 ≤ 15 holds. For the triangle inequality, u + v = (4, 2, 6), ‖u + v‖ = √56 ≈ 7.48, and ‖u‖ + ‖v‖ = 8, so 7.48 ≤ 8. Here u and v are not multiples, so both inequalities are strict.
chapters.trap: Dropping the absolute value: ⟨u,v⟩ ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖ is true but too weak, and many students then claim equality whenever the dot product looks small.
chapters.leave: Bessel's inequality and Parseval's identity need an orthonormal set, so they sit in 5.3.

chapters.idea: A set of mutually perpendicular unit vectors is automatically independent and acts like a coordinate system, and the orthogonal complement collects every vector perpendicular to a subspace.
chapters.depth: Define an orthogonal set (⟨uᵢ,uⱼ⟩ = 0 for i ≠ j) and an orthonormal set (⟨eᵢ,eⱼ⟩ = 0 for i ≠ j, ⟨eᵢ,eᵢ⟩ = 1). Prove that an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors is linearly independent and that it is a basis of its span. Give the coordinates in an orthonormal basis, cᵢ = ⟨u,eᵢ⟩, and the expansion u = Σ cᵢeᵢ. Define an orthogonal matrix by QᵀQ = I and note that it preserves lengths and angles. State Bessel's inequality Σ|⟨u,eᵢ⟩|² ≤ ‖u‖² and Parseval's identity Σ|⟨u,eᵢ⟩|² = ‖u‖² when the set is a full basis. Then define W⊥ = {v : ⟨v,w⟩ = 0 for all w in W}, prove W ∩ W⊥ = {0} and dim W + dim W⊥ = n, and state V = W ⊕ W⊥. Connect to Unit 2: the null space is the orthogonal complement of the row space.

figure.aria: A two-circle Venn diagram where the subspace W and its orthogonal complement share only the zero vector.

chapters.example: In ℝ³ let W = span{(1, 1, 0)}. A vector (x, y, z) is in W⊥ exactly when x + y = 0, so W⊥ = span{(1, −1, 0), (0, 0, 1)}. Then dim W = 1, dim W⊥ = 2, and 1 + 2 = 3 = dim ℝ³. The only vector in both is 0. The set {e₁ = (1,1,0)/√2, e₂ = (1,−1,0)/√2, e₃ = (0,0,1)} is orthonormal, and (2, 0, 3) = √2 e₁ + √2 e₂ + 3e₃.
chapters.trap: An orthogonal set containing the zero vector is not independent, so the theorem needs the words nonzero; and W ∩ W⊥ is {0}, not the empty set.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.1 and 5.2; Unit 2 for basis, dimension, null space and direct sums.
chapters.leave: How to build an orthonormal basis from a general one is 5.4; the projection formula is 5.5.

chapters.idea: Gram–Schmidt turns any basis into an orthonormal basis by subtracting from each new vector its parts along the vectors already fixed.
chapters.depth: Write the process explicitly. Set v₁ = u₁ and e₁ = v₁/‖v₁‖. For k ≥ 2, set vₖ = uₖ − ⟨uₖ,e₁⟩e₁ − … − ⟨uₖ,e₍ₖ₋₁₎⟩e₍ₖ₋₁₎, then eₖ = vₖ/‖vₖ‖. Explain why it works: the subtracted terms remove the components along the earlier directions, and the span of {e₁, …, eₖ} equals the span of {u₁, …, uₖ} at every step. Do full arithmetic in ℝ³ as the syllabi ask. Note that subtracting against the original uᵢ with the coefficient ⟨uₖ,uᵢ⟩/⟨uᵢ,uᵢ⟩ is an equivalent form. Mention in one line that modified Gram–Schmidt subtracts one direction at a time and loses less accuracy on a computer.

figure.title: Gram–Schmidt on three vectors
figure.aria: A vertical flow that normalizes the first vector, subtracts its part from the second, normalizes again, subtracts both parts from the third, and normalizes once more.

chapters.trap: Subtracting ⟨u₃,u₁⟩u₁ instead of ⟨u₃,e₁⟩e₁, or dividing by ‖v‖ instead of ‖v‖² when the projection is written with the original vectors.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.1 and 5.3; Unit 2 for basis and span.
chapters.leave: The projection formula and its geometry are 5.5; the same numbers become the matrix Q in 5.6.

chapters.idea: The point of a subspace closest to b is the projection of b onto it, and that turns an inconsistent system Ax = b into the solvable normal equations.
chapters.depth: Projection of b onto a single vector a is (⟨b,a⟩/⟨a,a⟩)a. For a subspace with orthonormal basis {e₁, …, eₖ}, the projection is p = Σ⟨b,eᵢ⟩eᵢ = QQᵀb, where Q has the eᵢ as columns. State and justify the best approximation property: ‖b − p‖ < ‖b − w‖ for every other w in the subspace, and the residual e = b − p is orthogonal to the subspace. List the projection matrix properties P = QQᵀ, P² = P, Pᵀ = P. Then least squares: minimise ‖Ax − b‖ over x, derive the normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb, and note they are solvable and unique when the columns of A are independent. Fit a straight line to three data points.

figure.title: Projection and least squares
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow from the target vector b to its projection p in the column space, then to the residual, then to the normal equations.

chapters.example: Fit y = c₀ + c₁x to (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 4). Then A = [[1,0],[1,1],[1,2]] and b = (1, 2, 4)ᵀ. AᵀA = [[3,3],[3,5]] and Aᵀb = (7, 10)ᵀ. Solving 3c₀ + 3c₁ = 7 and 3c₀ + 5c₁ = 10 gives c₁ = 1.5 and c₀ = 5/6 ≈ 0.833, so the line is y = 0.833 + 1.5x. The residual is (1/6, −1/3, 1/6), and Aᵀe = (0, 0)ᵀ, which confirms it is perpendicular to both columns.
chapters.trap: Writing the normal equations as AAᵀx = b or as Ax = Aᵀb; the correct left factor is Aᵀ on both sides, and the method needs AᵀA to be invertible.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.3 and 5.4; Unit 1 for solving systems; Unit 2 for column space.
chapters.leave: The pseudo-inverse and the SVD solution of least squares are 5.7; orthogonal diagonalization is in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Run Gram–Schmidt on the columns of A and the bookkeeping numbers form an upper triangular matrix, so A = QR.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it compact. State A = QR with Q having orthonormal columns and R upper triangular with rᵢⱼ = ⟨aⱼ, qᵢ⟩ for i < j and rⱼⱼ = ‖vⱼ‖ > 0. Show how the Gram–Schmidt formulas of 5.4 produce the entries. Distinguish the thin form (m × n with n columns) from the full form, in one line. Show that AᵀA = RᵀR, so a least-squares problem becomes Rx = Qᵀb, solved by back substitution. Do one full 3 × 2 example.

figure.title: QR from Gram–Schmidt
figure.aria: A flow from the columns of A through Gram–Schmidt to the factors Q and R, and then to solving a triangular system.

chapters.trap: Filling only the diagonal of R with the norms and forgetting the off-diagonal entries rᵢⱼ = ⟨aⱼ, qᵢ⟩, which are needed to rebuild A.
chapters.leave: Householder reflections and floating-point error analysis; the SVD in 5.7 is the other standard factorization.

chapters.idea: Every matrix, square or rectangular, splits as A = UΣVᵀ: a rotation, a stretch along perpendicular axes, and another rotation.
chapters.depth: State the SVD with shapes: A is m × n, U is m × m orthogonal, Σ is m × n with the singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ 0 on the diagonal, V is n × n orthogonal. Explain the computation: the eigenvalues of AᵀA (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix) are σᵢ², the columns of V are its orthonormal eigenvectors, and uᵢ = Avᵢ/σᵢ for σᵢ > 0, with the remaining u's filled by an orthonormal basis of the left null space. Show that rank A equals the number of nonzero singular values and that the condition number is σ₁/σₙ. Mention low-rank approximation in one line. Use the spectral theorem from Unit 4 as the reason this always works.

figure.title: Computing the SVD
figure.aria: A vertical flow from A to A-transpose-A, then to its eigenvectors giving V, then to the singular values, then to the columns of U, and finally to the factorization.

chapters.example: Take A = [[3,0],[4,5]]. Then AᵀA = [[25,20],[20,25]], whose eigenvalues are 45 and 5, so σ₁ = 3√5 ≈ 6.708 and σ₂ = √5 ≈ 2.236. Unit eigenvectors are v₁ = (1,1)/√2 and v₂ = (1,−1)/√2. Then u₁ = Av₁/σ₁ = (3,9)/(3√5·√2) = (1,3)/√10 and u₂ = Av₂/σ₂ = (3,−1)/(√5·√2) = (3,−1)/√10. So A = UΣVᵀ with U = (1/√10)[[1,3],[3,−1]], Σ = diag(6.708, 2.236) and V = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]]. Both singular values are nonzero, so rank A = 2.
chapters.trap: Taking eigenvalues of A itself instead of AᵀA; that shortcut is valid only for symmetric positive semidefinite matrices, and it fails as soon as A is not symmetric.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 (eigenvalues, symmetric matrices, spectral theorem) and chapter 5.3 (orthonormal bases).
chapters.leave: Numerical SVD algorithms, the full Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse theory, and image-compression case studies.
